subject: Civil Engineering
title: Fatigue: When Materials Get Tired
description: A quick, practical guide to Fatigue: When Materials Get Tired.

hook.text: Bend a paperclip back and forth enough times and it snaps. That's fatigue.

buildup.text: Repeated loading creates microscopic cracks that grow a tiny bit with each cycle.

discovery.text: Fatigue failure happens below the material's rated strength — surprise collapse.

twist.text: Bridges endure millions of load cycles from traffic. Fatigue is their silent enemy.

climax.text: Engineers inspect welds and joints for hairline cracks before they spread.

punchline.text: Even strong materials break if you bend them enough.

quiz.question: Why is fatigue failure particularly dangerous?
options: It only occurs in wooden structures
It happens at loads below the material's rated strength, without warning
It causes structures to melt from friction heat

details.summary: Fatigue is progressive cracking caused by repeated cyclic loading at stress levels far below the material's static strength. Microscopic cracks initiate at stress concentrations, grow with each load cycle, and eventually reach a critical size causing sudden fracture.
details.whyItMatters: Fatigue can cause failure at stresses well below the material's apparent strength. Bridge members, crane components, and aircraft structures all accumulate millions of stress cycles over their service lives.
takeaways: Fatigue cracks initiate at stress concentrations like notches, welds, and bolt holes
Crack growth is progressive and can be monitored through regular inspection
Design details that minimize stress concentration are critical to fatigue life

faq.question: Why can fatigue cause failure at stresses below the material's yield strength?
faq.answer: At microscopic stress concentrations, local stresses exceed yield even when average stress is low. Each load cycle advances a tiny crack by plastically deforming material at the crack tip.

faq.question: How is fatigue life estimated for structural components?
faq.answer: S-N curves relate stress range to the number of cycles to failure for standard detail categories. Miner's rule sums the cumulative damage from stress ranges of varying amplitude. Fracture mechanics methods predict crack growth rate from initial flaw size.
